[Um, yeah?]

The biggest risk, judging by how options traders are pricing likely moves in the S&P 500 (SPX), is around the midterm election, as UBS's chart shows.

But the S&P 500 has historically rallied an average of 6% from the end of September to the end of December in midterm election years, and an average of 14% from end September to end March, according to UBS.

"We see rising odds of a broadening in the equity market rally if the above catalysts turn out largely positive. Rising equity markets associated with rising correlations has historically resulted in stronger returns," they say.

UBS says the trade to make is to buy out of the money (OTM) call options on the S&P 500. OTM call options have a strike price above the current S&P 500 level and are bullish bet on the index that have greater risk and potentially greater reward.

There’s a really pronounced divide between people who are on the AI side of things and people who are on the biology side of things.  Even among people working in AI, the divide persists based on where they’re focused.

The AI side, adherents of scaling laws and the bitter lesson, believe that AI getting better means AI being more capable of novel discoveries in medicine (that go beyond discovering new drugs in well understood targets or speeding up dry lab work etc). 

The biology people think the idea of a bitter lesson in biology is kind of ridiculous and that regardless of AI’s capabilities it’s going to be at least 5-10 years until you could hope to reliably simulate human toxicology in silico (right now AI/ML can’t even reliably simulate in vivo studies like binding affinities or functional assays). 

Even the most AI pilled of them, who will list all the areas that AI can reduce the time spent on various areas, don’t think the concept of AI discovering novel targets or generating new understanding of causal biology is realistic in the near term. Most, in fact, will readily characterize the assumption that even an “ASI” level model could find cures hidden in our current understanding (without expanding that understanding with significantly more biological data) as patently false. 

This was a big part of why we wanted to experience it ourselves by using AI for a (very) small portion of what it can do in biology. It was both mind blowing and revealed some poignant insights into how different the problem of making AI better at something like coding is to the problems of biology. 

Even if it unlocked the ability to generate new molecules at a stunning pace, its simulation (in silico) of binding only had 49% accuracy. And if we wanted to improve that, we’d need to feed it back the data from the lab - data that took about 30x as long to get as it took to generate the molecules. And these were tests in a test tube (turn of phrase), imagine how long it would take if we wanted to improve the model with data that required recruiting humans and monitoring their reactions. 

Human biology is very complex, and adding a drug - especially a novel drug and doubly so for a novel drug acting on a novel mechanism - means mapping interactions that have nth-order-effects that we don’t have the data to predict. Virtual cells have made advancements enabled by AI, but the perturbations equate to a small fraction of the possible. 

This is before you even get into curing disease, especially uniquely human diseases. Brain function involves cellular identities that are unique to humans, meaning animal studies are of little use. 

How long does it take to understand what the side effects of chronic administration of a drug in humans are? AI can speed up analyzing the data, or designing the trial or even getting it approved…but it can’t make a 6 month trial complete in 3 months. 

I think its important to point out that significant advancements can be made in AI that contribute to biology, while also being realistic about how much it speeds up something as complex as curing a specific cancer or diseases of the brain.

Even the most AI pilled of them, who will list all the areas that AI can reduce the time spent on various areas, don’t think the concept of AI discovering novel targets or generating new understanding of causal biology is realistic in the near term. Even if it unlocked the ability to generate new molecules at a stunning pace, its simulation (in silico) of binding only had 49% accuracy. And if we wanted to improve that, we’d need to feed it back the data from the lab - data that took about 30x as long to get as it took to generate the molecules. And these were tests in a test tube (turn of phrase), imagine how long it would take if we wanted to improve the model with data that required recruiting humans and monitoring their reactions. 

Human biology is very complex, and adding a drug - especially a novel drug and doubly so for a novel drug acting on a novel mechanism - means mapping interactions that have nth-order-effects that we don’t have the data to predict. Virtual cells have made advancements enabled by AI, but the perturbations equate to a small fraction of the possible. 

This is before you even get into curing disease, especially uniquely human diseases. Brain function involves cellular identities that are unique to humans, meaning animal studies are of little use. 

How long does it take to understand what the side effects of chronic administration of a drug in humans are? AI can speed up analyzing the data, or designing the trial or even getting it approved…but it can’t make a 6 month trial complete in 3 months. 

I think its important to point out that significant advancements can be made in AI that contribute to biology, while also being realistic about how much it speeds up something as complex as curing a specific cancer or diseases of the brain.

This Apollo report, claiming AI has returned "zero financial payoff" outside of the Mag 7, is a complete non sequitur. 

They show that profit margins and revenue per employee is flat outside of the Mag 7, therefore the rest of corporate America is not seeing any returns to AI spend.

Who sees the problem with this analysis?

Obviously: this is not how you measure the contribution of a variable. You need to measure returns between companies that use MORE AI vs that use LESS AI. A flat aggregate like profit margins across all companies is totally incapable of answering this question.

Breaking out Mag 7 vs everyone else is also not the right unit of analysis. Mag 7 are mostly AI sellers, everyone else is mostly an AI buyer. 

Look at the backdrop. Interest rates are rising, oil is at $116, inflation is rampant, and consumer sentiment is a record low. If the AI buyers are holding onto their profit margins despite that, this is consistent with AI is actually buoying the economy.

TL;DR: the conclusion of this article is completely ass-backwards. Very strange writeup.

🚨🇫🇷 France is now borrowing at more than 5% over 10 years and consequences could be far more significant than markets currently anticipate - FT

📈 Despite rising bond yields, France remains far from a sovereign debt crisis but the spread between French and German 10-year bonds is hovering around 170 basis points. Moreover, when we convert five-year sovereign yields into US dollars using cross-currency swaps, stripping out much of the difference in monetary policy expectations, French debt shows a synthetic yield above 6% compared with 5% for the US. Even though, this is not the rate at which France actually borrows, it reveals a significant deterioration in the compensation investors demand to hold French government debt.

💰 With an average debt maturity of more than eight years, France benefits from a substantial buffer as higher interest rates do not immediately affect the entire outstanding debt stock. However, this buffer only delays the problem and doesn't eliminate it. The French government's interest bill is expected to rise from €62.6 billion in 2026 to €72.9 billion in 2027. With €340 billion in medium- and long-term bond issuance planned for 2027, net of buybacks, a sustained 100-basis-point increase in borrowing costs could translate into several billion euros in additional annualized interest expenses on new issuance alone. If rates remain elevated long enough, this could structurally weaken France's public finances.

🇪🇺 France's situation remains nowhere near the European sovereign debt crisis of 2011–2012, when Greek bond spreads reached several thousand basis points. However, France doesn't need to experience a Greek-style crisis to suffer a major deterioration in debt sustainability. Unlike the US, whose interest burden as a share of GDP is actually higher, France does not independently control its monetary policy. Some argue that worsening French economic conditions would push the ECB to act but there is no guarantee that a confidence crisis specific to France would trigger monetary easing across the entire eurozone.

⚠️ When borrowing costs remain elevated while economic growth is weak and primary deficits persist, stabilizing public debt requires fiscal adjustments. Those adjustments can themselves weigh on economic growth making fiscal consolidation even harder. France still has full access to capital markets and government bond auctions continue to attract investors but we may face a fiscal credibility crisis that gradually becomes entrenched.

➡️ I believe the main risk is that investors continue to finance France at a price that makes its fiscal trajectory increasingly difficult to sustain, and that doesn't require a spectacular sovereign debt crisis.

The current generation of models is already really good at coding. The next generation will be even better. As often happens, the capabilities are there before someone builds the harness to fully use them.

I think we’re going to get an OpenClaw moment for software replication. Someone will drop a simple harness that:

- Visits a software product with computer use, clicks everywhere, fills out forms and explores every workflow.
-Inspects the DOM, console logs, network requests, API responses and how state changes to figure out how it works.
-Turns those observations into tests covering the UI and the backend behavior it can observe.
-Writes a giant Markdown TODO and launches a swarm of agents to rebuild it.
-Uses the browser again to run the same workflows against both versions, compare results and keep fixing the differences.

Give it a URL, let it run. Software competition is going to get very close to perfect competition.

Never doubt the AI exponential, because it can catch up with your entire career while you’re still explaining why your profession is special.

Just listened to Cédric Villani, a Fields Medal winner, talking about how shocked he was by the progress of AI. Funny because I met him twice, including around 2018 when he was a Member of Parliament leading France’s AI mission, and we were already discussing how fast NLP was progressing with the new transformers.

France has 13 Fields Medals, second only to the US, and some of the brightest people I know come from that world. A lot of them have been caught by surprise despite following AI for years and using the products themselves.

I think it’s very hard to accept the exponential when it threatens something you’ve spent your entire life building, especially when your career is such a big part of your identity. You can see what’s happening to graphic designers or software engineers and still convince yourself that your own work will take another 20 years.

My guess is every intellectual profession will go through this, and honestly, even believing in the exponential doesn’t prepare you for the consequences. I work on this stuff all day, I expect progress to keep compounding, and I still struggle to imagine what that means a few years from now.

I don’t think nature has equipped us to really grasp exponential growth. We can understand the math and still struggle to imagine what it means for our own lives, even while watching it happen.

tweets.full_text:
We looked at each Texas site planning on-site power that falls under Governor Abbott’s Sept 21 directive, which tells TCEQ to stop issuing any permit tied to a datacenter until ERCOT finishes its review, and found six campuses, 8.7GW in all, needing air permits during the pause. (1/5)🧵

Our base case is that TCEQ resumes in December once ERCOT delivers its Dec 10 report, so the phases needing permits soon slip about a quarter and the rest of our forecast holds. Which campuses, phases and MW are exposed is in the Datacenter Industry Model. sales@semianalysis.com (5/5)

Because an air permit only gates the power plant, site work and any generation already permitted keep moving during the hold, so a three-month pause on issuance only becomes a delivery delay for a campus that has to start building its plant before the review ends. (4/5)

That 8.7GW is campus size rather than what gets delayed, since three of the six already have a first tranche of generation permitted and are only waiting on the expansion permit, while one has filed and is waiting and the other two haven’t filed anything yet. (3/5)

The directive matters because Abbott’s August pause only covered grid interconnections, so campuses building their own generation behind the meter were untouched and on-site power became the workaround, whereas TCEQ now confirms the freeze covers their air permits too. (2/5)
